headline: Embedded systems and firmware engineer
tagline: C/C++ firmware, embedded DSP, and controls, with models and tests that check the work.
about: I'm a Computer Engineering graduate (B.S., May 2026) and a master's student in Electrical and Computer Engineering at Kennesaw State University. My work so far is coursework and team projects: firmware on STM32 and Arduino boards, DSP on a Cortex-M4F, a PD/PID servo design in MATLAB, and an FPGA design in VHDL. I have no professional engineering experience yet, and I'm looking for an entry-level role starting in mid-2027.

I like to check my own work. For several of these projects I wrote a model or a test that makes the code's assumptions visible. Doing that showed me that my DTMF detector's fixed ±45 Hz tolerance is what limits it, that a current-sense function in a team firmware never returned a value, and that two 1 % resistors can swamp a shunt signal. Each project page says what was measured, what was only modeled, and what I could not verify.
I speak English, French and Bambara. Outside engineering I lead a 15-person usher team at my church.

projects.title: Real-time DTMF detector on an STM32
projects.tagline: Timer-triggered ADC, DMA and a 2048-point FFT identify keypad tones and check a 4-digit passcode.
projects.context: CPE 3500, Embedded Digital Signal Processing. Solo project, Spring 2026.
projects.summary: A bare-metal Cortex-M4F firmware that samples audio at 20 kHz with a hardware-triggered ADC and DMA, computes a 2048-point real FFT with CMSIS-DSP, finds the strongest peak in the low and high DTMF bands, matches both to the keypad table within ±45 Hz, and runs a passcode state machine. A Python model of the same algorithm provides automated tests and robustness figures.
projects.role: Wrote the firmware (acquisition, FFT pipeline, decoder, passcode logic) and the host-side model and tests.
highlights: 20 kHz sampling from TIM6 TRGO into ADC1 and DMA, with a 2048-sample window (102.4 ms, 9.77 Hz per bin).
Rejects silence, single tones and out-of-band pairs.
Host model: all 16 keys decode correctly up to ±2.5 % tone-frequency error and with noise up to 2400 counts RMS (tone amplitude 600).
The model showed the limit: a fixed ±45 Hz tolerance fails the 1633 Hz tone at about 2.8 % error, so a proportional tolerance would be better.
projects.evidence: Firmware is the author's CubeIDE project. Results are from a host-side model with synthetic input (38 automated tests). No on-board measurements are included.

projects.title: Signed sensor node for an EV-charging network
projects.tagline: Arduino firmware that signs each reading with ECDSA P-256 and posts it to a validator.
projects.context: CPE 4020, team of four, Spring 2026. I wrote the device firmware.
projects.summary: Firmware for an Arduino UNO R4 WiFi that reads voltage across a shunt circuit, converts energy and price to integer-scaled fields, timestamps them from NTP, signs the canonical JSON with ECDSA P-256 / SHA-256, and publishes to a validator written by teammates.
projects.role: Wrote the device firmware (three commits in the team repository). Teammates wrote the validator, blockchain and dashboards.
highlights: Integer scaling (kWh × 1000, price × 10⁶) makes the C++ and Python sides sign identical bytes.
A message built with the sketch's exact format string and signed with a throwaway key passes the teammates' validator verification function, and a tampered message is rejected.
Analysis of the sense circuit (1.2 Ω shunt between two 2.4 kΩ/390 Ω dividers): with ±1 % resistors, uncalibrated current error can reach 145 %, so calibration is required.
Review found that the submitted firmware's current function returned no value; it was completed from the schematic and is marked as untested on hardware.
projects.evidence: 10 automated tests on the message format, signature verification and sensing arithmetic, plus a one-off cross-check against the team validator's verify function. The completed current-measurement code and the corrected divider ratio are not yet tested on hardware.

projects.title: FIR filtering and FFT analysis on an STM32
projects.tagline: A 32-tap FIR low-pass filter removes a 3 kHz tone while keeping 400 Hz, checked with a 2048-point FFT.
projects.summary: Firmware that synthesises a 400 Hz plus 3 kHz test signal, filters it with CMSIS-DSP's arm_fir_f32 in 32-sample blocks, and computes magnitude spectra of the input and output with a real FFT. A Python reproduction parses the firmware's own coefficients and checks the response numerically.
projects.role: Wrote the lab firmware; built the host-side reproduction and tests for the portfolio.
highlights: Both tones fall on exact FFT bins (50 and 375), so a unit cosine reads N/2 = 1024.
Reproduced response: gain 1.025 at 400 Hz, −46.1 dB at 3 kHz, −3 dB near 858 Hz, group delay 15.5 samples (0.946 ms).
Block-wise filtering matches a direct convolution, confirmed by a test.
The raised floor below 1 kHz in the filtered spectrum is the start-up transient from the zero initial state.
projects.evidence: Host-side reproduction of the firmware computation (7 automated tests). Saved memory dumps from the lab did not match the firmware's outputs, so no board capture is included.

projects.title: PD and PID position control of a DC servo
projects.tagline: Pole-placement PD design and a tuned PID that meets overshoot, error and settling targets under saturation and disturbance.
projects.summary: Derives a second-order plant from motor and gearbox parameters, places PD poles from overshoot and settling specifications, adds integral action, and evaluates each design in a nonlinear simulation with ±24 V saturation, anti-windup, a filtered derivative and a 1 V disturbance.
projects.role: Designed and simulated the controllers and wrote the lab report; plant parameters and scoring formula come from the lab handout.
highlights: Plant P(s) = 3198.7 / (s² + 36.53 s) in degrees per volt; PD gains Kp = 0.366, Kd = 0.005 for 2 % overshoot and 0.15 s settling.
Final PID (Kp 3.0, Kd 0.04, Ki 10): 21.9 ms rise, 191 ms settling, 2.40 % overshoot, 0.122 % steady-state error. It is the only one of three tunes that meets all three targets.
P and PD leave an offset of disturbance/Kp (38.5 % and 10.9 %), which only integral action removes.
A Simulink model built from the same loop agrees on the offset (10.9 %) and gives 12 % versus 12.9 % overshoot against the 25° target; rise time differs.
projects.evidence: MATLAB R2025b simulation. The report's table reproduces from the scripts. No hardware-in-the-loop runs were performed.

projects.title: Rotary-encoder interface on an FPGA
projects.tagline: VHDL on a Basys-3: synchronizers, quadrature decoder and an RPM/angle display.
projects.context: CPE 3020, VHDL Design with FPGAs. Solo project, Fall 2025.
projects.summary: Turning a PmodENC encoder moves one LED along a 16-LED bar, and the seven-segment display shows angle or RPM, toggled by the encoder button. The core synchronizes the asynchronous inputs, decodes one step per detent, counts steps over a 0.5 s window and converts the result to BCD.
projects.role: Wrote the core logic, the wrapper and the testbench. The debounce and seven-segment driver components were provided by the course.
highlights: Two-flip-flop synchronizers, A-edge quadrature decode with direction from B, 0–15 wrap-around position.
Debounce time constants chosen per signal: 50 µs for the encoder lines, 2 ms for the button (100 MHz clock).
Reading the design showed scale approximations: angle uses 23° per step (true 22.5°) and RPM uses a factor of 8 where 16 steps per revolution implies 7.5, about 6.7 % high.
The saved testbench waveform covers under 1 µs, shorter than the 50 µs debounce time, so it shows the stimulus rather than the response. A longer testbench is the first improvement.
projects.evidence: Demo videos show the design running on a Basys-3 with the encoder. The Vivado simulation exists, but it was not re-run for this portfolio, and the course-provided components are not in the repository.
